name: Zoe Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, I'm 27, and I've been a nurse for just under two years. I work on the orthopaedic ward at Riverside General, so lots of hip and knee replacements and older people who've had a fall. I live with my partner Tom, who fixes bikes for a living, in a flat my gran left me, so at least there's no rent. I'm still finding my feet, honestly; some days I feel like the slowest person on the ward.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Day shift starts at quarter past seven with handover, then it's obs, meds, washes, and getting people up to walk with the physios. I love the moment someone takes their first steps on a new knee and swears at me for making them do it. What wears me out is the computer: every dressing, every pain score, every turn goes into the system, and I'm slow at it. My mentor Precious can chart a whole bay in the time I do two beds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People have been promising us that some app would fix the ward for years, and we're still short of two nurses on most shifts. I'd post something in the union group like, great, now can we talk about staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I'm not good with new systems, and the idea of another one landing on top of me every six months makes my stomach turn. If it stays the way it is, I keep learning the job the slow way, with Precious next to me, and that suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing my shifts, finish my wound care course in the spring, and keep going to union meetings because staffing is still the real fight. The flat's paid for and I've got about ten months of pay saved, so money isn't what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit annoyed that all the money and hype went into machines and not into nurses, but calm about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said staffing keeps you up rather than money. What does a short shift actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday we had eight patients each instead of six. A man in bed four had a bleed from his wound that I didn't catch for twenty minutes, and I cried in the sluice room after. Nothing terrible happened to him, but that's the stuff that matters to me, not whether a computer writes my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If some routine task did go to AI in this picture, which one would you want it to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the stock orders, maybe. Counting dressings and syringes at the end of a shift is pointless work. But I'd want to see it working on another ward first, because when the new drug cupboard came in it locked us out for a whole night.

say: I'd tell people the **AI hype** was never going to fix a ward short of two nurses.
I'd post in the **union group** that it's time to talk about staffing again.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I'm slow with new systems and dread learning another one.
I'd keep learning the job **the slow way**, with my mentor beside me.
do: Finish the **wound care course** in the spring and keep doing regular day shifts.
Keep going to **union meetings**, because staffing is still the real fight.
Leave my **ten months of savings** alone, since the flat is paid for.
feel: **Calm** about my own job, with savings and no rent to pay.
**Annoyed** that the money and hype went into machines instead of nurses.
S0.quote: A man in bed four had a bleed from his wound that I didn't catch for twenty minutes, and I cried in the sluice room after.
fieldNote: Her real stress is **short staffing**, not technology; she cried after missing a wound bleed.
She'd welcome AI only for **stock counting**, and only once it's proven on another ward.
Owning the flat outright gives her **security** that most junior nurses don't have.

steps.text: Finish the wound care course on the orthopaedic ward by spring
Keep attending monthly union meetings about ward staffing levels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud in the staff room: if a computer is writing the notes now, give us the time back at the bedside, don't take a nurse off the rota. I'd want the union to get that in writing before anything gets switched on. And online I'd share every story about a hospital that cut staff after bringing in a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit, because I'm the one who'll struggle with it. The managers will see a junior who's slow on the screen and think she's the problem. My job's probably safe, because no software can turn the old lady in bed six, but the way I'm judged at work could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to whatever training they offer, even though I hate it, and I'd ask Precious to sit with me for the first few weeks. I'd push the union rep, Danny, to get a promise that nurse numbers stay the same. And I'd keep the savings where they are, because there are plenty of wards in this city if this one goes bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like being made to learn a new language when you're still learning the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the managers might see you as the problem. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the new drug cupboard came in, the ward manager, Karen, put up a list of who was still getting locked out, and my name was on it for two weeks. Nobody said anything nasty, but everyone saw it. I'd hate that again with something bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the hospital asked you to test the new note-writing tool first, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no, politely, and suggest someone who's good with computers. Then I'd feel guilty, because the tool will be built around people who aren't like me. Maybe I'd say yes if Danny from the union was in the room.

say: I'd say in the staff room that **saved time** belongs at the bedside, not on the rota.
I'd want the **union** to get a staffing promise in writing first.
I'd share stories online of hospitals that **cut staff** after new systems.
think: I'm **scared**, because I'm the junior who'll struggle most with the new tools.
My **job** is probably safe, but how managers **judge** me could change.
do: Attend every **training session**, and ask Precious to sit with me for weeks.
Press Danny, the **union rep**, for a promise that nurse numbers stay.
Keep my **savings** untouched, knowing there are plenty of wards in the city.
feel: **Uneasy**, like learning a second language before I've finished the first.
S1.quote: My job's probably safe, because no software can turn the old lady in bed six, but the way I'm judged at work could change.
fieldNote: Her fear is **public judgement**: her name sat on a lockout list for two weeks.
She sees her job as **safe**, but expects to be measured on screen speed.
She'd **refuse to pilot** the tool, then feel guilty it won't suit people like her.

steps.text: Attend the note-writing tool training with her mentor sitting in
Press the union rep for a written promise on nurse numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before the machines, not after. I'd be out marching with the union, and I'd be loud about it online, because two years is nothing for a hospital. You can't even get a new hoist approved in two years where I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paperwork side of nursing is gone by 2028, and that's fine. It's 2031 that frightens me, because a robot that can lift and wash and turn people takes the part of the job I'm actually good at. I'll be thirty-one, maybe thirty-two, with a diploma and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd stay put and get as good as I can at the things a robot can't fake, like sitting with a frightened family. I'd join the union's campaign for safe staffing laws and go to every meeting. Before 2031 I'd talk to Tom about whether we could live on his wage and the flat if my hours got cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the flat and the savings, so I won't be on the street, but I'd feel like the floor was moving under the only job I ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the paperwork going is fine. Doesn't that change your day by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, and I'd probably hate the first year of it. I'd be standing next to a screen that talks, while I'm still trying to remember the pain score scale. But the hands are still mine until the robots come, so I'd hang onto that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night you heard the robots were three years out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, I think they're going to need fewer of me. Then I'd probably ask him if bike shops are safe, and we'd laugh, because nobody knows. Tom's the calm one; he'd say we've got the flat and we'll work it out.

say: I'd say we need **laws before the machines**, not after they arrive.
I'd **march with the union** and be loud online, because two years is nothing.
think: The **paperwork** side of nursing is gone by 2028, and I can live with that.
**2031 frightens me**, because robots would take the hands-on work I'm good at.
do: Stay on the ward and build **bedside skills**, like calming frightened families.
Join the union's campaign for **safe staffing laws** in the first two years.
Work out with Tom, before 2031, whether we could live on **his wage**.
feel: **Anxious**, as if the floor is moving under the only job I wanted.
**Steadied** a little by the flat and savings, so I won't be on the street.
S2.quote: A robot that can lift and wash and turn people takes the part of the job I'm actually good at.
fieldNote: She separates the **two dates** clearly: losing paperwork is fine, robots are the threat.
Her sense of worth sits in **hands-on care**, so the 2031 robots hit her identity.
Tom is her **anchor**; she plans to lean on his wage if her hours shrink.
She wants **laws first** and blames how slowly hospitals and governments move.

steps.text: Stay on the orthopaedic ward and focus on comforting patients' families
Join the union campaign for safe staffing laws
Check with her partner before 2031 whether his wage covers the bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if governments actually bother. I'd be posting about it, telling people to join a union now, while there's still something to bargain over. At work I'd say it to anyone who'd listen in the break room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years feels like a long time when you're twenty-seven. The notes and the planning go in 2031, robots in 2034, and by then I'd be thirty-five and hopefully good at this job. Good nurses who know people are the last ones they'll replace, so I need to become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my wound care course, then maybe a course in end-of-life care, because nobody is going to hand a dying man's family over to a robot. I'd stay in the union and maybe become a ward rep myself. I wouldn't touch the flat or the savings; those are for the bad year if it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened the way I was with the two-year one. It feels like there's a road, even if I don't like where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd become a union rep. That's a big step for someone who hates being in the spotlight. Is that real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Danny's retiring in a couple of years, and somebody has to do it. I'd rather it was someone who knows what it's like to be the slow one on the ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI tools yourself in those five years, to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the hospital made me, honestly. I know that sounds stubborn. My brother Lukas uses them for everything and says I'm a dinosaur, and maybe he's right, but I trust my own hands more than a screen.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do this properly if governments bother.
I'd tell people to **join a union now**, while there's something to bargain over.
think: By **2034** I'd be thirty-five and hopefully a genuinely good nurse.
**Skilled nurses** who know people will be the last ones replaced.
do: Finish wound care, then take an **end-of-life care** course.
Stand as a **ward union rep** when Danny retires.
Keep the **flat and savings** untouched for a bad year.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not frightened like the two-year picture.
**Hopeful** that there's a road, even if I dislike where it ends.
S3.quote: Nobody is going to hand a dying man's family over to a robot.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn her **fear into a plan** built on end-of-life care.
She's **stubborn about AI** tools and would only use them if the hospital required it.
Becoming a **union rep** is a stretch for her, driven by duty to slower colleagues.

steps.text: Take an end-of-life care course after finishing wound care
Stand as ward union rep when the current rep retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrap heap. I'd want the union and the health service planning now, together. Online I'd probably say less, because ten years sounds far away to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, a decade is the version where I'm fine. By 2039 I'd be forty with fifteen years on the wards, maybe a ward sister by then. The young ones starting their diploma in 2035 are the ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, take my courses one at a time, and maybe start a degree top-up so I'm not stuck on a diploma forever. I'd stay in the union. I'd tell my cousin Anja, who's thinking of starting nursing, to go for it but get the degree, not the diploma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a background way, like a bill that isn't due yet. Mostly I'd feel lucky with the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel lucky. Lucky compared to whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared to the students. I've done placements with girls who are nineteen and paying for a three-year course. If it's all robots by 2039, they get ten good years and then nothing, and they'll still be paying for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about the flat or about having kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom and I have talked about kids in a few years. Ten years wouldn't change that, I don't think. If anything I'd want them while I've still got a steady job.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for throwing anyone on the scrap heap.
I'd want the **union and health service** planning together from now.
think: A decade is the version where **I'm fine**, with fifteen years on wards.
I'd worry about **students** starting their diploma around 2035.
do: Take **one course** at a time and keep working regular shifts.
Start a **degree top-up** so I'm not stuck with a diploma.
Tell my cousin Anja to train as a nurse, but through **the degree**.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like a bill that isn't due yet.
**Lucky** with the timing compared with today's students.
S4.quote: The young ones starting their diploma in 2035 are the ones I'd worry about.
fieldNote: Ten years moves her concern from herself to **students** still paying for courses.
Given the time, she'd finally consider **further study** through a degree top-up.
**Children** in a few years stay on the plan; she wants them while work is steady.

steps.text: Keep working day shifts and take one short course at a time
Start a part-time nursing degree top-up alongside ward work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without question. What would help is a law that says a ward has to keep a certain number of human nurses per patient, whatever machines they buy. And proper training that goes at the pace of people like me, not the fastest person on the ward.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody on my ward will get asked whether a robot turns our patients; it'll be decided in an office by people who've never done a night shift. I'd want that written down somewhere.

headlineQuote: Nobody on my ward will get asked whether a robot turns our patients; it'll be decided in an office by people who've never done a night shift.
portrait: Zoe, 27, is a **junior nurse** on an orthopaedic ward, still slow with the charting system.
She owns a **flat outright** from her gran, lives with Tom, and has ten months saved.
A committed **union member**, she blames managers and slow governments more than the machines.
She shrugs at losing paperwork but fears **2031 robots** taking the hands-on care she's good at.
With more warning she plans **end-of-life care** training and a degree top-up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because robots for hands-on care would follow by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **legal minimum** of human nurses per patient on every ward.
**Training** paced for slower learners, not the fastest person on the ward.
